en: Supplementary Notes to the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*, Volume One.
Compiled by Dharma Master Pútài of Lùān. Supplementary Note on the Nature of Objects and Direct Perception:

"Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding objects of nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) penetrates all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). This means that among the three types of objects, the first five consciousnesses relate only to...
Regarding the nature of the object as a condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore,
all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are equally pervasive [in relation to these].
Regarding the objects [of cognition], there are three types of natures. "Nature" (xing) refers to reality.
These are constituted by the eight dharmas—the real sense organs and their objects, as well as the subject and object.
Thus, there exist objects that are real in essence and consist of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga).
This means that this object arises from its own real seeds and possesses a real substantial function;
it is a presently existing real dharma,
which is precisely the *ālambana-vijñapti-mātra* (object-only consciousness).
If, among the two types of transformation, the first five consciousnesses undergo causal transformation (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*),
they therefore take as their object only the ineffable specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Consequently, the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that take purely imaginary objects (*pratibimba*) as their domain are exclusively transformations through conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
It is solely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Since it is solely direct perception when cognizing objects,
it clearly and directly realizes all objects.
Therefore, it takes only real objects as its conditions.
This consciousness is common to all three natures— wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—
because the nature of the five consciousnesses is not always uniform.
The explanation is found below. There are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
namely, perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
For notes on inference and non-apprehension, see below.
This explains direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone.
"Direct" (*pra*) means manifesting;
it is so called because it apprehends its object with immediate clarity.
"Measurement" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the act of measuring,
because it establishes the definition [of an object].
When the mind and mental factors take an object as their focal point, [this occurs].
When [an object] is clearly and distinctly manifested, free from obscuration and other impediments,
the attainment of the object's own nature (*svabhāva*) is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) pertains to the object and "perception" (*pramāṇa*) pertains to the mind, [then this definition holds].
Some belong to both mind and body;
some currently belong to the sense faculties,
while their measure belongs to the mind.
Regarding the three types of analysis— tatpuruṣa (dependent), karmadhāraya (occupying the same case),
and bahuvrīhi (possessive)—
the term "essence" (*tattva*) refers precisely to the essence of the mind and mental factors as correctly understood by non-conceptual wisdom.
That is to say, when direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) engages its object, it is free from verbal designations, categories, and erroneous conceptualization;
this is termed non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Regarding the nature of this wisdom as direct perception, the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* states that there are four types.
First, the five sense-consciousnesses;
second, the simultaneous mental consciousness;
third, the self-verifying portions (svasaṃvedanabhāga) of all minds and mental factors.
The four universal mental applications (*sarvatraga-manasikāra*): these four are all objects of direct realization by the mind and are free from conceptual discrimination.
"The three—eye, ear, and body—reside in two stages": this refers to the stages (*bhūmi*) of the five sensory consciousnesses.
That is to say, there are three [stages] in the desire realm: food, sleep, and sexual desire; the stage of the five destinies living in a mixed manner;
and the stage of rapture and bliss born of seclusion in the first dhyāna of the form realm.
Since the three higher dhyānas lack both vitarka and vicāra, they are not included.
Consciousness does not arise because the dharmas of the earth element are devoid of vitarka and vicāra and are undefiled.
This verse-line is an elliptical abbreviation that includes the two consciousnesses of the nose and the tongue.
One realm and one stage:
namely, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the stage of the five destinies living in a mixture (*pañcagatimiśravāsin*).
This is because the higher dhyāna heavens lack substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Edible food has the three factors of odor, flavor, and tangibility as its substance.
Since edible food is absent,
these two consciousnesses do not arise.
Regarding those who lack this nutriment:
since edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is something the dhyāna heavens loathe,

[the mental factors] are the five universal, the five object-specific, the eleven virtuous, the two great [ground] factors, and greed, hatred, and delusion— these refer to the mental factors associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because they always arise in dependence upon the mind,
are associated with the mind,
and are bound to the mind.
Possessing these three meanings, it is like property belonging to oneself;
hence it is called "what belongs to me" (*ātmīya*).
This is precisely the corresponding *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Regarding the statement that the first five consciousnesses lack only the indeterminate mental factors among the six categories,
it is said that there are five universal factors. Among them,
attention (*manasikāra*) has the nature of being able to arouse the mind.
Its function is to draw the mind toward its object.
This single dharma possesses two powers:
first, when the mind has not yet arisen, it arouses it; second, [it sustains it].
Second, once the mind has arisen, it draws [the mental factors] toward the object.
Contact (*sparśa*) has the nature of causing the mind and mental factors to touch the object;
its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
Feeling (*vedanā*) has as its nature the experiencing of objects that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neither;
its function is to give rise to desire.
Furthermore, it is said to cause the mind to arise with the characteristics of joy, sorrow, or equanimity.
Perception (saṃjñā) is that which can establish the boundaries of its own object;
its nature consists in grasping the image of an object,
and its function is to designate various names and expressions.
That is to say, it is only by establishing the defining characteristics of the boundaries of an object that one can subsequently give rise to various names and expressions.
Volition has the nature of causing the mind to engage in purposeful activity.
Its function is to employ the mind toward virtuous categories and so forth; that is,
it can apprehend the characteristics of the correct causes and other factors regarding objects,
and direct the mind itself to perform virtuous and other such actions.
It is called "pervasive" because it can function throughout all four types of objects and within the mind; that is,
it pervades the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the nine stages, and all times.
Therefore, this name is established.
There are also five object-specific mental factors, namely:
desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Desire (chanda) has the nature of longing for an object of pleasure and functions as the basis for diligence.
There are three types of objects of pleasure.
The object that is delightful,
the object that is sought,
and the object that is intended for contemplation.
Third, the explanation of correct resolve (*adhimokṣa*):
Resolve has the nature of confirming and maintaining a determined object,
and its function is to be unshakeable.
Mindfulness has the nature of causing the mind to clearly remember an object previously experienced;
its function is to serve as a basis for concentration.
Concentration has the nature of causing the mind to focus intently on the object of observation without distraction.
Its function is to serve as the basis for knowledge.
Wisdom has the nature of discerning the objects under investigation,
and its function is to sever doubt.
They are called "distinctive objects" because they arise by taking distinct objects as their respective conditions.
Regarding the eleven wholesome [mental factors], the verse says:
Wholesome refers to faith, shame, and dread;
The three roots of non-attachment and so forth,
diligence, tranquility, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming—
these alone are associated with a wholesome mind and are thus called a "wholesome mind."
That which is called faith (śraddhā) has as its nature a deep acceptance, aspiration, and desire for what is real, virtuous, and capable, characterized by purity of mind;
its function is to counteract lack of faith and to delight in the wholesome.
However, there are three kinds.
First is conviction in actual existence,
which refers to the profound faith and acceptance regarding the reality and principles of all phenomena.
Second, faith in possessing virtue,
which means having deep faith and delight in the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels.
Third, faith in possessing capability.
This refers to having deep faith in the power of all mundane and supramundane virtues to be attained and accomplished; because one gives rise to aspiration,
it serves as the antidote to the mind of lack of faith.
It is the delight in realizing and practicing mundane and supramundane virtues;
"patience" (kṣānti) refers to resolute conviction (adhimukti),
which is the cause of faith.
"Delightful desire" refers to aspiration;
it is the fruit of faith.
This nature is lucid and can purify the mind and its associates.
Just as the water-purifying jewel can clarify turbid water,
so too does shame (*hrī*)— which has the nature of honoring and respecting the noble and virtuous by relying on the power of one's own mind—
have the function of counteracting lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and bringing unwholesome conduct to rest.
"Self" refers to one's own person;
"Dharma" refers to the teaching.
It means: "I, with such a body, understand such a Dharma."
It is the nature of shame (*hrī*) to feel remorse for committing various evils.
It relies on worldly power and has as its essential characteristic the light rejection of violence and evil.
Its function is to counteract the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and to bring about the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
That is to say, when people of the world revile and censure others, this is called worldly power;
they slight and reject those who are violent and evil,
and they do not associate with those who possess wickedness.
One refrains from performing actions that consist of unwholesome dharmas.
Non-greed is characterized by non-attachment toward existence and the requisites of existence.
Its function is to counteract greed and to perform wholesome deeds.
Non-hatred has the nature of being without malice toward suffering and the instruments of suffering.
Its function is to counteract ill-will and to perform wholesome deeds.
Non-delusion has the nature of clear understanding regarding all phenomena and principles;
its function is to counteract ignorance and to perform wholesome deeds.
Vigor (*vīrya*) has the nature of being courageous and resolute in the tasks of cultivating the wholesome and abandoning the unwholesome;
its function is to counteract laziness and bring wholesome qualities to fulfillment.
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) has the nature of being free from heaviness (*dausthulya*), bringing the body and mind into a state of composure and adaptability.
Its function is to counteract lethargy and effect a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, it is said that being free from heaviness is called lightness.
Harmony and fluency are called "tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*).
It refers to being capable and fit, and being able to undertake and receive [tasks],
because it causes the body and mind— the bases of experience— to abandon heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*) and attain serenity.
Non-negligence has the nature of being diligent in the three roots regarding that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be cultivated;
its function is to counteract negligence and to bring to fulfillment all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.
In short, this heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the function of guarding and cultivating based upon the aforementioned diligence and the three roots;
it has no separate essence apart from those four factors.
As for equanimity (*upekṣā*):
Its nature is to cause the mind to abide in equanimity, rectitude, and effortlessness by means of the three roots of diligence;
its function is to counteract restlessness and to bring about peaceful abiding.
This is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
This name is given because it is distinguished from the equanimity within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
It causes the mind and its associates to become even through equanimity,
at which time the mind is freed from both dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
The initial mind is equanimous;
the subsequent mind is upright;
the final [mind] is effortless.
This single dharma is also the four dharmas;
for that which is able to bring about tranquility is precisely these four dharmas.
That which causes tranquility is the meaning of mental equanimity.
Regarding "non-harming":
Its nature is non-hatred, which does not inflict harm or affliction upon sentient beings;

its function is to counteract cruelty and to exercise compassion. Of these ten factors, the first eight are substantial entities, while the latter three are provisional designations. Among the "eight great" [defilements] mentioned in the scriptures—greed, hatred, and delusion—[the first two are included therein].
These defiled mental factors comprise twenty-six types in total.
Within the first five consciousnesses, there are only thirteen fundamental afflictions and three of the secondary afflictions.
Among the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
ten of them comprise twenty categories in total,
divided into three grades: small, medium, and great.
The first ten, beginning with anger (*krodha*), are the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*);
they do not associate with the five sensory consciousnesses.
Only the two intermediate derivative afflictions [do so].
Together with the eight great [afflictions] and the secondary ones,
these belong to the aforementioned five;
they are termed "secondary afflictions" (upakleśa).
Because it is of the nature of an outflow (*niṣyanda*) corresponding to the distinctions in the states of its fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*),
it arises simultaneously with its own kind and pervades both natures throughout all defiled minds.
These three meanings, when all present, are termed "great";
when one is present, they are termed "middling";
and when none are present, they are termed "small."

Regarding the statement "two natures," it refers to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured (*nivṛta*). Regarding the statement "four natures" in the three-fascicle *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they are:
the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The desire realm possesses all four [categories];
the formless and form realms possess only three, as they exclude the unwholesome nature;
thus, the ten dharmas such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth are excluded.
Because they arise individually,
they lack simultaneous arising with their own kind;
being exclusively unwholesome, they lack both the pervasive and the defiled natures.
Since they lack the *nivṛta* (obscured) type and do not pervade all defiled minds, they are termed "minor" (*parīttānuśaya*).
These ten are associated with the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, *ahrīkya* (lack of shame) and *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread) are not explained here;
they are included within the category of those that arise together as their own kind (*svajāti-sahabhū*).
Regarding *ahrīkya*:
Its nature is to disregard one's own dharma and to reject the virtuous and good with contempt;
its function is to obstruct the growth of shame (*hrī*) and to give rise to unwholesome conduct.
As for lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*):
Its nature is to disregard the world’s esteem and to be violent and evil;
its function is to obstruct a sense of shame and to give rise to unwholesome conduct.
Restlessness (*auddhatya*), moreover, has as its nature that which causes the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its objects.
Its function is to obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*) and calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Lethargy (*styāna*), moreover, has the nature of rendering the mind incapable of functioning with respect to its object;
its function is to obstruct pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) has the nature of being unable to endure, delight in, or desire [the truth], virtue, and capacity; it takes mental impurity as its essence.
Its function is to obstruct the pure mind and to cause one to fall into dependence.
Laziness (*kausīdya*) has the nature of indolence regarding the practice of cultivation and abandonment within the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Its function is to obstruct diligence and increase defilement.
Heedlessness (pramāda) has as its nature the failure to guard against or cultivate the categories of the defiled and the pure, and the indulgence in laxity;
its function is to obstruct non-heedlessness, serve as a basis for the increase of evil and the diminution of the wholesome.
Lack of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) has as its nature the inability to clearly remember various objects of focus;
its function is to obstruct right mindfulness and to serve as the basis for distraction.
Regarding this lack of mindfulness:
Because the mind is distracted.
Regarding this "loss of mindfulness," some say:
It is subsumed under one part,
because it is mindfulness associated with afflictions. According to another interpretation:
It is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that because this is a portion of delusion, delusion causes the loss of mindfulness.
There is an interpretation that both are subsumed under one part each,
because the two preceding passages are stated by way of ellipsis.
Distraction has the nature of causing the mind to wander among various objects of focus.
Its function is to obstruct right concentration and to serve as a basis for faulty wisdom.
That is to say, one who is distracted...
Because it gives rise to unwholesome wisdom (*kuprajñā*),
non-apprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) has the nature of erroneous understanding regarding the object under observation.
Its function is to obstruct right knowledge and to constitute transgression.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are three of the six root afflictions.
Greed has existence as its object;
it is characterized by defiled attachment and functions to obstruct non-greed and to produce suffering. Hatred has suffering as its object.
Hatred has the nature of increasing resentment toward the instruments of suffering;
its function is to obstruct non-hatred and to serve as the basis for unease and unwholesome conduct.
Delusion has the nature of being confused and obscured regarding all phenomena and principles.
Its function is to obstruct non-delusion and to serve as the basis for all defilements;
the remaining three [characteristics] are explained in detail elsewhere.
As for why the sixth consciousness is considered the locus of the fundamental afflictions:
This is because it is capable of producing latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Why is it not associated with other [factors]?
Because they are mutually contradictory.

The five consciousnesses share a common dependence on the pure material sense-faculties (*rūpaprasāda*). This statement that the five consciousnesses are named after "pure matter" refers to the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*);
their essence is not a defiled phenomenon (*kliṣṭadharma*).
Because they are exclusively pure, neutral, and indeterminate (avyākṛta),
the five consciousnesses are named according to their respective faculties; thus,
they collectively possess these five meanings.
It is said that "relying" (yi) belongs to the category of "auxiliaries" (zhu).
As a verse states:
"Relying is one of the five meanings."
If one were to provide an explanation [of the compound],
it means that consciousness, which relies upon the sense faculty, assists the faculty; thus,
like "root" (*mūla*) and so forth, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
"Consciousness produced by the faculties" (indriya-ja-vijñāna) is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound.
Alternatively, it may be called "consciousness that is produced from the faculties.
This serves as another example.
"Nine conditions for seven and eight, with favorable factors adjacent": this refers to the principle of consciousness arising through nine conditions.
The nine conditions are:
space, light, the sense organ, the object, attention, discrimination, the support of defilement and purity, the fundamental support, and the seed.
"Space" refers to the empty space between the sense organs and their objects.
"Light" refers to the illumination of the sun, moon, and lamps.
"Organs" refers to the faculties upon which the eight consciousnesses rely.
"Object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the objects perceived by the eight consciousnesses.
"Attention" (*manasikāra*) is the attention among the five universal mental factors.
"The basis for discrimination" (*viniścaya-āśraya*) is the sixth consciousness; the first five consciousnesses take the sixth as their basis for discrimination.
The six consciousnesses take the first five as their gates of clarity;
the basis for defilement and purity is the seventh consciousness. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"All consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing: namely, the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the continuous flow (*pravāha*), and the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the manifested form (*nimitta*)."
In Sanskrit it is called *nirgata*,
which here means "flowing forth.
This refers exclusively to the uninterrupted continuity of the subtle and hidden seeds and manifestations of the three phases of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, it is called "streaming forth.
Because the initial karma-consciousness arises conditioned by ignorance,
it is said to be "birth."
Because it continues through long kalpas,
it is called "abiding" (sthiti),
until it reaches the diamond-like [samādhi].
In samādhi, one realizes perfect enlightenment and severs the fundamental ignorance of a single thought-moment;
this is called the "flowing stream.
It is the cessation of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
This means that the objects and mental states of the other seven consciousnesses are coarse and manifest;
therefore, they are called "aspects" (*nimitta*).
Although the seventh consciousness is subtler than the sixth when compared to the eighth, it is still considered coarse relative to the latter.
Because it possesses four afflictions, it is also called "coarse.
It takes the manifestation-consciousness as its basis; when its own seeds and various objective conditions combine, the seven consciousnesses arise as its characteristic.
Birth and long-term habitual perfuming are called "characteristics" (*nimitta*).
Abiding in them involves gradually subduing and severing [the afflictions] from their derivative forms back to their fundamental source, until the seventh stage is perfected.
This is called the cessation of characteristics.
Based on the former arising and ceasing, one establishes the basis for delusion and awakening;
based on the latter arising and ceasing, one establishes the basis for defilement and purity.
This refers to the establishment of the distinction between defilement and purity by dividing phenomena into those that are long at the beginning and short at the end.
The fundamental basis is the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
The seed-condition refers to the direct productive seed;
among the nine conditions, it is the seed-condition.
Among the four conditions, these are the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The nine objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are the four object-conditions.
The remaining seven of the nine are the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This is the domain of the sovereign eighth consciousness;
its preceding and succeeding moments of cessation and arising are immediate within its own kind,
and the power of the projecting cause and the projected result are equal.
Although this verse is concise and cryptic, it encompasses the theory of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra).
Thus, the verse says:
"Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions."

The ear-consciousness arises solely from eight conditions, excluding the condition of light. The nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses arise from seven conditions, excluding the two conditions of space and light. Regarding the latter three [consciousnesses], they refer to the six, seven, and eight [conditions] respectively; regarding the five, four, and three [objects], they refer to the conditions.
If the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are added,
one more is appended to each starting from the beginning;
thus they are said to be five, four, and three.
The sixth consciousness has five conditions for its arising:
namely, the sense organ as condition and the mental object as condition.
This refers to the eighteen bases (*dhātu*) as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for mental attention (*manasikāra*);
it is one of the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors associated with the fundamental conditions.
This refers to the seeds within the ālayavijñāna as conditions;
these are the direct productive seeds of the sixth consciousness.
As for the three conditions of the seventh consciousness:
The seed-condition (*bīja-pratyaya*).
That is, the seventh consciousness acts as the direct generative seed-condition for mental attention (*manasikāra*).
See the note above.
Since both the root-condition and the object-condition are the eighth consciousness,
it is said that "it transforms depending on that and takes that as its object.
Regarding the eighth consciousness arising from the four conditions:
That is to say, the root condition;
that is, the object-condition of the manas;
and the conditions of the seeds, the root-body, the vessel-world, and mental attention.
This is one of the five types of objects.
As for the "seed-condition," it refers to the seeds that are directly produced by the eighth consciousness.
The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to that which,
as each preceding moment of consciousness has already ceased, opens up a space and induces the subsequent moment to arise, such that there is no interval between them.
If these conditions are added to the eight consciousnesses, the eye-consciousness has ten,
and so on up to the eighth consciousness, which possesses five.
For what reason do the various consciousnesses arise only by depending upon conditions?
Because conditioned phenomena depend upon causes and rely upon conditions,
they do not arise when these are lacking;
therefore, while conditions are many, their cessation is rare and constant.
This verse is an abbreviated summary of the latter three [perceptions];
therefore, it does not mention that these three possess all the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*).

"Combining the three and separating the two to observe the mundane world" refers to the fact that the visual and auditory consciousnesses apprehend their objects through separation (*viprakṛṣṭa-grahaṇa*).
The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through conjunction.
When observing that the visual faculty capable of cognition is the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*), it refers to the eye and so forth.
The five consciousnesses and all mental factors take the "object-aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their objective support; these are the five sensory objects, such as visible form and the rest.
Or it may be argued that since the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear apprehend their objects from a distance,
those objects must exist outside the mind.
What is meant by "consciousness-only"?
How much more so for those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and others,
who all claim that various phenomena truly exist externally to the mind.
If this were so, it would not only deviate from the tenet of Vijñaptimātra;
how could it possibly not also contradict the doctrines of the Hīnayāna and external schools?
Nevertheless, the verse speaks of "separation."
This refers to the sense organs and their objects.
Specifically, the eighth self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) transforms into the two divisions of seeing (*darśanabhāga*) and appearance (*nimittabhāga*).
The seeing division is the aspect of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
This refers to the phenomena of the body, the sense organs, and the objective world.
When it is said that the visual and auditory consciousnesses apprehend objects external to the sense organs,
how could they ever be separated from the essence of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) which undergoes transformation?
If one distinguishes between the known and the unknown locations,
and differentiates between the impaired and the unimpaired faculties,
then it can be seen that objects are either separated from or conjoined with the faculties.
Therefore it is said:
"One speaks of separation and union based on the sense organs perceiving objects;
one discusses 'consciousness-only' based on the mind apprehending objects."
Because it excels in being free from grasping and utilization,
it is established as a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
"The foolish find it difficult to distinguish between consciousness and the faculties"— this refers to the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle who follow the Dharma of the ignorant.
One does not realize that the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) each possess their own seeds and actualities (*bīja-vartamāna*),
and thus assume that the faculties and consciousness arise from one another.
In reality, the seeds and actualities of the faculties can only guide the seeds and actualities of consciousness.
This means that while the sense faculties can be said to serve as conditions for the arising of consciousness,
it cannot be said that consciousness possesses its own seeds capable of producing itself; therefore,
because the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have not yet been eliminated.
To lack understanding of the Dharma is due to shallow wisdom and a coarse mind; because of this,
one does not believe in the Mahāyāna teaching of Vijñaptimātra.
This commentary states that the seeds and manifestations of the sense faculties and consciousnesses are distinct.
Fearing that beginners may still harbor doubts, I shall explain further.
For the faculties are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
The object-aspect (nimittabhāga) is that of the eighth [consciousness];
consciousness is a mental dharma (caitasika),
and the subject-aspect (darśanabhāga) is that of the eighth [consciousness].
This is because matter and mind are distinct.
Although the sense organs belong to the category of matter,
they serve as the immediate objective part (sākāra-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness.
The eighth consciousness alone possesses both meanings of "appropriation" (*upādāna*):
namely, "grasping" (*udgrahaṇa*) and "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*). Furthermore, "grasping" has two senses:
first, the eighth consciousness takes [the body] as its own essence through appropriation; second, being equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it maintains [the body] so that it does not disintegrate.
Feeling (*vedanā*) also possesses two meanings: apprehension and sensation.
It apprehends [the object] as its objective domain and causes the arising of sensory cognition.
It cannot be compared to insentient objects such as the six external sense-fields;
therefore, the eighth consciousness and the five sense organs are both of the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
The mental factors associated with the five consciousnesses possess all three natures.
This is because the natures of the sense faculties and consciousnesses are different.
Furthermore, the faculties can illuminate objects while consciousness can cognize objects;
this is because the functions of the faculties and consciousnesses are different.

Generally speaking, although the five sensory consciousnesses lack conceptual discrimination at the level of the sense bases (*mūla-vikalpa*), they do possess subsequent recollective discrimination (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*) but lack deliberative discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*); therefore,
they are constantly intermingled and difficult to distinguish.
Therefore, for those whose minds are deluded, the Buddha opens his heart to them by teaching the aggregates (skandhas);
for those deluded regarding form, he opens [his heart] to them by teaching the bases (āyatanas);
and for those deluded regarding both, he opens [his heart] to them by teaching the elements (dhātus).
From the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka* until the *Śūraṅgama*,
these three categories have been expounded countless hundreds of thousands of times;
yet Ānanda still spoke in terms of "the mind knowing" and "the eyes seeing."
Therefore, the Buddha questioned him regarding whether he could see through the gate;
his intention was that the mind perceives by means of the sense organ,
just as a person sees objects by means of a lamp.
From this it can be known that the distinction between the sense faculties and consciousness is difficult to discern.
"Observing emptiness through transformed appearances" refers exclusively to subsequent attainment; this indicates that the first five [consciousnesses] perceive the conventional and see emptiness.
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) refers to the transformation and manifestation [of consciousness]; "aspects" (nimitta) refer to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga);
and "contemplation" (darśana) refers to the subjective aspect of the perceiving faculty (darśanabhāga).
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of the emptiness-eye is suchness (tathatā);
the phrase "only the subsequently attained" (pṛṣṭhalabdha) excludes the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna),
because it relies solely upon the material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya).
The subsequently attained wisdom does not directly take suchness as its object because it is a wisdom involving conceptual discrimination;
it cannot directly take the non-conceptual principle as its object, but arises through deliberation.
Therefore, this emptiness is the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

Even within the state of fruition, it does not directly designate reality; that is to say, even the five untainted consciousnesses (*anāsravapañcavijñāna*) in the stage of Buddhahood cannot yet directly take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object.
Because fundamental wisdom relies upon the mental faculty (manas-indriya),
it directly takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object;
because subsequently attained wisdom relies upon the material faculties (rūpīndriya), it possesses conceptual discrimination.
The reason one cannot directly take True Suchness (tathatā) as an object is said to be because of "subsequently attained" [knowledge].
Since the fundamental [knowledge] must precede the arising of the first five [consciousnesses],
if the fundamental is absent, how could there be the subsequently attained?
Because it belongs to that same category and because it apprehends the same object,
this verse refutes the tenets of other teachers.
According to the school of Ananta, among the first five reasons, it is already established that the uncontaminated transformation consciousness takes suchness as its object;
this is because the perceived and perceiving aspects are of the nature of universal construction (parikalpita-svabhāva),
while the self-verifying aspect is of the nature of dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva).
Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) directly perceives suchness (*tathatā*),
because it lacks the conceptualizing aspect (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that constitutes a "view.
This is why Master Huihu protected [the teaching] by using this sentence to refute [the opponent's position].

"When the perfectly luminous [wisdom] first arises, it becomes the three types of emanated bodies that cease the wheel of suffering. This refers to the mental factors associated with the five sensory consciousnesses when they reach the fruit through the exhaustion of their causes.
This immediately constitutes the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*),
which manifests three types of bodies to bring to rest the wheel of suffering for sentient beings.
That is to say, within the state of Buddhahood, once the eighth consciousness has been transformed into the untainted, pure white consciousness (*anāsrava-śukla-viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The mental factors associated with this [state] then become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom,
manifesting suddenly before one; therefore,
it is said that "the first stage has been initiated."
Then the first five consciousnesses immediately become untainted (*anāsrava*);
hence it is said that they "become untainted.
Regarding the "three types of transformation bodies":
The mental factors of the five consciousnesses immediately constitute the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*),
which manifests the three types of bodies.
These three types of bodies are, among the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies, specifically the Nirmāṇakāya.
The capacities of those for whom this transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is intended vary in degree of excellence; therefore,
there are likewise three types of transformation bodies that can manifest accordingly.
The thousand-fathom great transformation body manifests for Bodhisattvas of the four stages of application (*prayoga*) of the Mahāyāna;
the small transformation body of one *zhang* and six *chi* manifests for Bodhisattvas of the three stages of accumulation (*sambhāra*) of the Mahāyāna;
and it manifests in accordance with the various types for those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Three Vehicles universally encompass all beings, and those in the six destinies alike receive its benefits.
Some say that the first five consciousnesses constitute a mental complex (*citta-viprayukta*) associated with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Manifesting in bodily form to benefit sentient beings—
why, then, does it first state that the eighth [consciousness] achieves the outflow-free state?
It is because when perfect luminosity first arises, it corresponds precisely with the mental factors of the eighth consciousness, which is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
In essence, the first five sense organs are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by the eighth consciousness.
Since the fundamental consciousness that manifests them has become untainted (*anāsrava*),
the five sense organs it manifests likewise become untainted.
It can give rise to the five faculties.
Once these have become untainted (*anāsrava*), the five consciousnesses they produce consequently become untainted as well.
Someone says:
Since it has already been stated that the eight consciousnesses are transformed to form the four wisdoms, why does it instead speak of the "associated mental factors" (*cittapakṣa*)? It says:
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:
These four categories comprehensively encompass all conditioned merits of the Buddha-ground without exception.
These are the categories associated with the eight, seven, six, and five consciousnesses that were previously impure;
by transforming them, one successively attains wisdom.
Although it is not consciousness itself, it evolves in dependence upon consciousness;
because consciousness is primary, it is said that "consciousness evolves and attains" [the state].
Furthermore, in the state of being with outflows (sāsrava), wisdom is weak while consciousness is strong.
In the state of outflow-free realization (*anāsrava*), wisdom is predominant while consciousness is subordinate.
To encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness,
it is taught that the eight consciousnesses are transformed to attain these four wisdoms.
The term "transforming consciousness" (pravṛtti-vijñāna) used hereafter should be understood according to this principle.

Regarding the three natures (trisvabhāva), the three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the three objects (triviṣaya): this statement indicates that the sixth consciousness is universally applicable to all three natures, all three means of valid cognition, and all three objects.
The character "penetration" (tong) runs through both the preceding and following sections.
Regarding the three natures (trisvabhāva):
"wholesome" (kuśala) carries the meaning of being favorable and beneficial.
It accords with correct principle and benefits oneself and others;
that which is unwholesome is contrary to and detrimental to these aims.
To contravene correct principle and to cause harm to oneself and others—
there is no such thing as that which is "unspecified" (avyākṛta). There is no [such thing].
Regarding "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*):
it refers to that which cannot be definitively categorized within the categories of good or evil.
Therefore, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are explained here by means of the meanings of conformity and opposition, as well as benefit and harm.
It is further said:
that which is conducive to and beneficial for both worlds is called a wholesome nature;
that which is contrary to and detrimental to both worlds is called an unwholesome nature.
That which cannot be designated as either a pleasant or unpleasant fruit is termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
That which is both itself and its fruit desirable is termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*);
the unwholesome (*akuśala*) is the opposite of this.
That which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant and cannot be definitively categorized is termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, these three natures are explained here in terms of the outflows (*āsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) across the three periods of time.
As for the "three measures" (*trividha-pramāṇa*):
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) explains the preceding section;
now, however, only inference (*anumāna*)—and not the other two types of valid cognition—is explained. As for inference:
Inference across realms is without error.
That which is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists in the mind but lacks objective reality;
this is because such inference fails to reach its mark.

Regarding the sixth consciousness, there are five types; first is the "solitary" [consciousness] within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wherein the mental consciousness takes the objects of concentration as its sphere.
These objects of concentration consist of both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
Furthermore, there are matters that are extremely concise and extremely remote:
namely, the various forms within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) consisting of matter and those produced by mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
as well as the two types of independent [consciousnesses] occurring in the state of distraction.
It is like depending on forms derived from sensation and forms belonging to the sphere of phenomena that arise through conceptual construction—
such as depending on flowers in the sky, reflections in a mirror, or painted images.
Those that arise are all subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Third, the independent consciousness within dreams, which takes dream-objects as its cognitive domain.
Fourth, the clearly manifest mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
It shares the same objects of perception as the first five consciousnesses,
namely the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The "five distracted mental consciousnesses" refers to the scattered mental consciousness.
It arises from the derangement of the five faculties;
it is like seeing blue as yellow when suffering from a fever,
which is not the visual consciousness itself.
This is the intended meaning:
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) during meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
the independent, distracted mental consciousness consists of inference (*anumāna*) and is not the other two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The two consciousnesses— the dreaming consciousness and the distracted consciousness—
are both non-valid cognitions (*apramāṇa*).
The clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) encompasses all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is evident that inference is manifold rather than few; this is seen in the preceding passage on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Here, we shall correctly explain inference, which is distinct from the other two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
First, the definition will be explained.

If the solitary, scattered mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cognizes its object without error, it is called inference (*anumāna*). When inferential cognition is not fixed upon its object, it is termed non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).
Thus, "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the essential nature of the cognizing mind itself.
If the arising of the mind and mental factors through inference based on an object as their cause is termed "inference" (anumāna) in general,
then if the inference pertains to the object and the valid cognition (pramāṇa) pertains to the mind, [this distinction holds].
The object of inference (*anumeya*) is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound;
if both [the subject and the property] belong to the mind.
"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is capable of comparison.
"Non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*) does not mean "not [valid cognition]," but rather "that which is not valid."
This is another name for error.
When the mind and mental factors take an object as their focal point,
if they do not cognize the object as it truly is and instead give rise to a distorted understanding, that is error.
It is called "non-means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*).
It is not identical to "means of valid cognition.
This is an example of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Next, to explain their essential natures:
inference (*anumāna*) has as its nature the mental states and mental factors of correct conceptual cognition;
non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) has as its nature the mental states and mental factors of false, deluded, and erroneous cognition.
Regarding the "three objects":
the nature-object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) has already been explained in the preceding text.
It is now re-explained here because it is relevant to the discussion of the two objects—the shadow and the substance.
Regarding "real objects" (xingjing):
these consist of the eight dharmas formed by actual sense organs and their objects, as well as the matter resulting from meditative concentration (samādhi-phala-rūpa);
all of these arise from their own actual seeds.
Thus, the five preceding [consciousnesses] and the eighth [consciousness], as well as the sixth consciousness when it takes actual material objects (*rūpa*) as its objective referents—
being devoid of verbal designations and free from conceptual estimation— are termed "objective spheres" (*xingjing*).
Furthermore, fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) taking suchness as its object is also this [same] sphere.
Because it functions spontaneously and without conceptualization,
it is of two kinds.
Regarding the first category of objective spheres (viṣaya):
these are precisely those previously mentioned.
Regarding the second category, none of the aforementioned meanings apply at all.
The aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is defined as an objective realm (svabhāva-viṣaya) from the perspective of its being derived from a primary substance.
Because it is designated by way of metaphorical expression, there is also a second type, the "aspect-bearing objective realm" (sanimittaka-viṣaya), which likewise has two kinds.
Regarding the true aspect-bearing objective realm:
When the mind takes as its object the intermediate image-part (nimittabhāga) within [the same] mind,
arising continuously from both ends,
it is called a "true connected-with-essence" (zhendai-zhi) cognition.
Regarding that which resembles the "substantial" (sadravya): because the mind takes form as its object,
the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* arises solely from one end of the *darśana-bhāga*, arising as a transformation that carries [the image].
This is called "resembling a substantial object.
There are also two types of "solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*).
Regarding what is called a "solitary image without a substantial object":
This refers to the objective images (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the sixth consciousness when it takes as its objects empty flowers, rabbit horns, the past and future, and so forth.
These objective images arise from the same seeds as the sixth consciousness itself;
they lack any external substance such as empty flowers.
Regarding those that have a substantial basis (saviṣaya) or are mere shadows (pratibimba):
these are the sixth [consciousness] taking the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs as its objects;
all of these arise by relying upon a substantial basis.
Its image-part (nimittabhāga) also arises from the same seed as the seeing-part (darśanabhāga);
it is also called "solely reflected" (kevalapratibimba).
The object serves as its objective support (ālambana).
Consciousness acts as the perceiving subject;
each has its own essence.
Regarding the essence of the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), see the commentary above.
Regarding those that can take objects:
with the exception of the manas-consciousness,
the remaining seven all have their own mind and mental factors as their substance.
The object of solitary reflection (duoying-jing) has as its essence the provisional aspect of the perceived portion (xiangfen) transformed by the sixth consciousness’s seeing portion (jianfen);
its perceiving subject consists of one's own mind and mental factors.
The object with a substantive core (dai zhi-jing) has as its essence the provisional aspect of the intermediate stage transformed [between the subject and object].
That which acts as the cognitive object (ālambaka) consists solely of the mind and mental factors of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Regarding the statement that these six [consciousnesses] access three types of objects:

when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) accompanying the five [sensory consciousnesses] does not engage in conceptualization, it apprehends the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of its object.

This constitutes the objective realm of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). When taking minds and mental factors as objects, they constitute the objective realm of the "carrying of substance" (*sadravya-ālambana*).
When taking dharmas that lack substantial reality as objects, they constitute the objective realm of the "solitary image" (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*).
This is stated with reference to the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
In the state without outflows (*anāsrava*),
all eight consciousnesses take three types of objects as their cognitive domain, because they universally cognize both the conventional (*prajñapti*) and the substantial (*dravya*).
Therefore, the verse says:
"The objective realm of intrinsic nature does not follow the mind;
the solitary reflection arises solely from the seeing-part."
The "mixed" [consciousness] penetrates both the manifest and the fundamental;
it is said that the nature-seeds and so forth exist according to their respective applications.
The sixth consciousness has five types.
Excluding the consciousness of a distracted mind and the consciousness in dreams,
which take only "solitary shadows" as their objects,
the remaining three types of consciousness all take all three kinds of objects.

This means that when the clear and distinct mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the five objects as its conditions, these five objects are actual entities within the state of sudden perception; they constitute the objective realm (svabhāvaviṣaya).

However, if subsequent moments of thought take those five objects as conditions to perceive qualities such as square, round, long, or short—these are merely conventional forms (prajñaptirūpa) and thus possess a substrate.
The "solitary image" (*duoying*) is also called "resembling that which possesses a substrate" (*sidadizhi*).
The solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in its distracted state also takes three kinds of objects;
most of these are solitary images.
Because it universally takes as its object all phenomena of the three periods of time, whether they possess substance or lack substance;
when it takes as its object the currently active mind and mental factors within one's own continuum,
this constitutes an object with substance.
If one takes as objects the five sense faculties of one's own body or the mind and mental factors of another person,
these are solitary images;
they are also termed "resembling a substantial entity."

Furthermore, the independent manovijñāna (consciousness) in its initial moment takes a small portion of the five sense objects as its object; taking actual matter (rūpa) as its object is also termed a "nature-object" (svabhāva-viṣaya). The manovijñāna within meditative concentration likewise universally takes all three types of objects as its objects.
This means that because it universally takes as its object all phenomena of the three periods of time— whether they possess substantial reality or lack it—
it is an object consisting solely of mental images;
furthermore, it can also take as its object the currently functioning mind and mental factors of one's own continuum.
This refers to objects that carry their own objective spheres (*saviṣaya*).

Furthermore, even in the states of meditative concentration with outflows (*sāsrava-samādhi*) prior to the seventh stage, one can still give rise to the five consciousnesses perceiving the five sense objects;
these are precisely "objective objects" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).
"The movement within the three realms is easily known" refers to the three realms mentioned above.
"Movement" (*cakra*) means revolving.
This states that the movement of the sixth consciousness back and forth through the three realms is easy to know because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is manifest and predominant.
It alone is supreme in initiating physical movement and uttering speech.
Among the fifty-one mental factors (caitta) associated with the mind, it is only this sixth consciousness that [possesses them] within these eight consciousnesses.
Because all mental factors (caitta) are fully present and do not contradict one another,

the ten universal factors (sarvatraga), the ten object-specific factors (viniyata), the eleven wholesome factors (kuśala), the six roots (mūla), the six afflictions (kleśa), and ten among the secondary afflictions (upakleśa)— namely, the three common ones and the seven great ones— have been explained above.

Only the seven mental factors—the three consisting of the root afflictions of pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), together with the ten minor [afflictions] and the four indeterminate factors—constitute these seventeen dharmas.
Herein lies the explanation of their meanings.
Regarding "pride" (*māna*):
Its nature is the exaltation of oneself in relation to others.
Its function is to obstruct non-conceit and to give rise to suffering.
Specifically, when one possesses pride, the mind does not become humble toward those who possess virtue.
Because one undergoes all manner of suffering through this endless cycle of birth and death,
"doubt" (vicikitsā) is characterized by indecision regarding the principles of the Truths.
Its function is to obstruct the absence of doubt regarding wholesome qualities;
for when there is hesitation, wholesome states do not arise.
Wrong view has the nature of defiled wisdom that erroneously speculates upon the principles of the truths.
Its function is to obstruct right view and to bring about suffering;
for those with wrong views undergo much suffering.
These views comprise five types in total:
namely, the view of a self-identity, extreme views, false views, and adherence to views and precepts.
Regarding "minor derivative [afflictions]," such as anger:
It is defined as having the nature of being provoked by an immediately present, harmful object.
Its function is to obstruct non-anger and to involve the grasping of weapons;
"weapons" refers to arms and implements.
Because those who harbor resentment frequently manifest violent and evil bodily *kāyavijñapti* (informative action),
it is said that "hatred" (*upanāha*) has the nature of harboring malice without relinquishing it and binding oneself to a grudge, preceded by anger (*krodha*).
Its function is to obstruct non-resentment and to cause feverish affliction.
For one who is bound by resentment,
it is impossible to maintain forbearance, and they are thus constantly afflicted by feverish distress.
Resentment (*krodha*) and enmity (*upanāha*) are both parts of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Concealment (*mrakṣa*) has the nature of hiding one's own committed transgressions out of fear of losing profit and reputation.
Its function is to obstruct the absence of concealment, regret, and distress.
This is because one who conceals their transgressions will inevitably experience regret and distress, and thus lack peace of mind.
It consists of two parts: greed and delusion.
As for vexation (*pradāśa*), its nature is that of violent malice and resentment, preceded by anger and enmity, which pursues and contacts [its object].
Its function is to obstruct non-annoyance and [the absence of] insect stings;
it is also a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*).
As for envy (*īrṣyā*):
It is characterized by a nature of envy and jealousy due to an inability to endure the prosperity of others, being devoted to fame and profit.

Its function is to obstruct non-envy and to produce sorrow and distress. As for what is meant by "envy": *Note: The term translated as "envy" is *īrṣyā*. It refers to a mental state that feels resentment toward the excellence, status, or success of others.*
Because hearing of the prosperity of others brings deep sorrow and distress, resulting in a lack of peace and stability,
it is also a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*).
As for what is called "miserliness" (*mātsarya*):
Its nature is that of being secretive and stingy, unable to give away the wealth of the Dharma to which one is attached.
Its function is to obstruct non-stinginess and the practice of accumulation.
That is to say, one who is miserly...
Because the mind is largely base and harsh, and because one accumulates wealth and teachings and is unable to relinquish them,
this belongs to the category of greed.
As for "deceit":
Its nature is that of deceitful hypocrisy for the sake of profit and reputation;
its function is to obstruct non-deception and right livelihood.
This refers to those who are hypocritical and deceptive.
Because one harbors ulterior motives and frequently manifests unreal matters of wrong livelihood,
this is a derivative of greed and delusion; thus,
it is called *śāṭhya* (deceit).
For the sake of deceiving others,
it feigns extraordinary deportment and has guile as its nature;
its function is to obstruct non-guile and the receiving of instruction.
That is to say, one who is crafty and devious,
in order to deceive others and comply with the requirements of the times,
falsely devises expedient means to win over their favor.
Alternatively, it is a portion of greed and delusion because one conceals one's own faults and fails to submit to the correct instruction and admonition of teachers and friends.
As for "harming": [it refers to...]
Its nature is the lack of compassion for sentient beings and the intent to harm them;
its function is to obstruct non-harming and to cause affliction.
That is to say, it is that which possesses harmfulness.
Because it afflicts others,
it is subsumed under one portion of hatred (*dveṣa*).
As for what is called "haughtiness" (*mada*):
Its nature is to give rise to deep attachment and intoxicated arrogance toward one's own prosperity.
Its function is to obstruct non-conceit and serve as a basis for defilement.
Regarding this "intoxicated arrogance" (māna):
Because it causes all defiled phenomena to grow,
this is a category of craving;
that is to say, it refers to non-intoxication.
This is precisely non-attachment (*alobha*).

As for the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), they consist of the ten factors beginning with anger (*krodha*) along with the three factors of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*);
these are merely distinct states within the fundamental [afflictions].
The remaining seven are of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Regarding the four indeterminate [factors],
the verse says:
The indeterminate [mental factors] are remorse and sleep;
the two pairs of vitarka and vicāra each have two types.
These differ from the five categories of mental factors mentioned previously.

These four factors—concentration (*samādhi*), pervasiveness (*vyāpi*), the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—as well as time (*kāla*) and stage (*bhūmi*), are all indeterminate.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* distinguishes the five types [of objects] by means of the "four kinds of universality" (*catuḥsarvatraga*). It states:
The universal [mental factors] possess all four;
the object-specific ones possess only the first two;
and all wholesome [factors] possess only one.
That is to say, the defilements of all stages are entirely without indeterminate [factors];
there is only one [category], namely, those that pertain to all [stages].
Regarding the term "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*):
the prose commentary states that remorse refers to the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).
Bad conduct (*kaukṛtya*) is the cause;
regret (*kaukṛtya*) is its essential nature.
Since the nature is itself the cause, [the two are identical].
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Regret (kaukṛtya) refers to 'badly done' (akukṛta);
this is the meaning of cause and effect."
It is defined as having the nature of remorse for actions performed through evil intent,
and its function is to obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*). Because *śamatha* can cause the mind to abide, it is called "stillness."
Sleep has as its nature the lack of self-mastery over the body, extreme mental obscurity, and lightness;
its function is to obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*).
That is to say, the inclusion of objects within the mind through *vipaśyanā* is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*);
its essential nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
As for this sleep that can cause the body and mind to become equal, there is the "sleep without consciousness."

when in fact a state without mind is not called sleep?
For "sleep" (middha) is a mental factor (caitta) capable of causing the cessation of mental activity.
Since that [sleep] lacks any substantial entity, how could there be its function?

Vitarka (investigation) is of the nature of seeking, causing the mind to move coarsely toward the objects of mental discourse with a sense of urgency.
Vicāra (analysis) is of the nature of examining, causing the mind to move subtly toward the objects of mental discourse with a sense of urgency.
The function of these two dharmas is, in both cases, to serve as the basis for the states of mental and physical well-being or ill-being.
Regarding the "object of mental discourse," it refers to the objects apprehended by the mind, which for the most part depend upon names and expressions.
Therefore, it is called the "object of mental verbalization.
Both of these take a portion of the wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) as their essence.

Because wisdom is urgent and coarse, if that were the case,

Master Tongzhao explained that there is both a secondary and a primary application.

When good or evil arises according to the occasion, they are respectively assigned [to it]. This means that when the sixth consciousness encounters a wholesome object, it is associated with wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*).

The natures, elements, feelings, and so forth, follow the transformation of consciousness.

Among the eight consciousnesses, its mode of activity is the most preeminent.

For example, it is like a fish submerged in a deep pool that reveals its presence by stirring the waves.

Just as the four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom as their essence,
they are called "foundations of mindfulness" because wisdom is proximate to mindfulness;
since they are thus adjacent, [they are so named].
When the [action] is not identical to itself,
it is called "without the same object" (*anabhidheya-karmaka*);
this meaning applies to the other two types of analysis as well.
First, proximity as a dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*):
for example, when someone is living near Chang'an,
and another person asks:
"Where do you reside?
He replied,
"I reside in Chang'an."
This person is not from Chang'an;
because he is near Chang'an, he is said to "dwell in Chang'an.
This is a case of adopting another's name by way of association.
Furthermore, there are two types of proximity: proximity by dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*) and proximity by possession (*bahuvrīhi*).
For example, as when asking, "In what place does the person dwell? [the answer is given in terms of the location].
The answer was:
"Chang'an.
This was done by taking the name of another place in its entirety to designate the person's name.
This is indeed the place of Wealth (Yūcai).
Because it is near Chang’an, it is also called Línjìn (Neighboring).
The verse says:
Used for oneself and used for others;
used for both oneself and others;
it applies to both [categories] and to all three types.
These are the six kinds of explanations.
